newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Doctors confident as Yeltsin heart operation nears.
newsitem.headline: Doctors confident as Yeltsin heart operation nears.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin's doctors are ready to cope with any problems as a deadline for surgery nears but believe he can finish his full term in office, a senior doctor was quoted as saying on Tuesday.
Sergei Mironov, the 48-year-old head of the Kremlin medical centre, told the daily Komsomolskaya Pravda newspaper that preparations for Yeltsin's heart operation were going according to plan.

"If everything goes well, I mean the operation itself and the period after it, I am confident -- touch wood -- that Boris Nikolayevich (Yeltsin) will be able to work fully throughout his presidential term, and longer," Mironov said.
"Believe me, he is a strong and a powerful person."

Yeltsin, 65, was reelected on July 3 for a second term in office. But the president has spent most of the period since the election out of the Kremlin -- vacationing, resting or getting ready for open heart surgery.

Presidential press spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said on Monday that preparations for the operation had reached their final stage and that doctors had cancelled all Yeltsin's planned meetings while they carried out a final round of tests.
Yeltsin had two heart attacks last year and doctors say he probably had a third one before the July 3 runoff election.

Michael Rees, a cardiologist at the Bristol Royal Infirmary in Britain, said tests which could force doctors to cancel Yeltsin's meetings might include "invasive" investigations such as inserting a tube to examine arteries properly.

But he said cancelling meetings for a full week was a little unusual. "Of course this is speculation, but maybe they are going to do the surgery before they announce it. Or they could be gearing up for alternative surgery such as angioplasty, which involves inserting a balloon to stretch arteries," he said.
Rees said Yeltsin's doctors had to weigh up the advantages of an early operation with the risks on operating on someone who had not fully recovered from a heart attack.
"The longer you delay, the longer you run the risk of a further heart attack," he said.

Yeltsin's announcement on September 5 that he needed an operation to bypass clogged cardiac arteries broke a Kremlin tradition of secrecy about the health of its leaders and reignited a bitter power struggle among ministers and aides.

Yeltsin last week appealed to his aides and ministers to work together. "There have been enough struggles for influence, fights for jobs, criticism and electioneering. It is time to work," he said in a radio address.

Mironov said there had been no changes to a timeframe set for Yeltsin's operation, which would take place either at Russia's main cardiological centre or at the elite Central Clinical Hospital where Yeltsin was treated in the past.
The planned deadline of 6-10 weeks set by doctors on September 25 could mean the operation being held as early as next week -- or it could mean a delay until late November.
Mironov said Yeltsin, who was working for around two hours a day in the Barvikha sanatorium outside Moscow, had never had kidney problems and problems with his liver were "due to age".
He said problems with Yeltsin's blood were being sorted out.
"There has been a problem and we have not concealed it. But we are sorting that out and I think that we are on the right path," he said.
